name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Increasing order of radii of isoelectronic species

questiontext.text: Consider the isoelectronic species, \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\), \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\). The correct order of increasing length of their radii is ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The given species are \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\), \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\), and \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\). Each ion has 10 electrons and therefore constitutes an isoelectronic series.

Step 2: Assumptions and Governing Principles
For isoelectronic ions, the number of electron shells and electron-electron shielding are comparable. The ionic radius is governed primarily by the effective nuclear charge, which is determined by the number of protons in the nucleus (atomic number \(Z\)). A higher nuclear charge exerts a stronger electrostatic pull on the surrounding 10 electrons, contracting the electron cloud and decreasing ionic size.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Evaluation
Determine the atomic number (nuclear charge) of each element:
Oxygen (\(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\)): \(Z = 8\)
Fluorine (\(\mathrm{F^{-}}\)): \(Z = 9\)
Sodium (\(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\)): \(Z = 11\)
Magnesium (\(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\)): \(Z = 12\)
As the nuclear charge increases, the ionic radius decreases progressively: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}} < \mathrm{Na^{+}} < \mathrm{F^{-}} < \mathrm{O^{2-}}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
The ion with the highest positive charge and greatest nuclear charge (magnesium ion) has the smallest radius, while the divalent anion with the lowest nuclear charge (oxide ion) has the largest radius. Hence, the correct increasing order of radii is \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}} < \mathrm{Na^{+}} < \mathrm{F^{-}} < \mathrm{O^{2-}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Identification of element that is not actinoid

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not an actinoid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The f-block elements consist of two series: the lanthanoids (4f-series), which span atomic numbers 58 to 71 (following lanthanum, \(Z=57\), often taken as 57 to 71), and the actinoids (5f-series), which span atomic numbers 90 to 103 (following actinium, \(Z=89\), often taken as 89 to 103).

Step 2: Evaluation of Elements
Uranium (\(Z = 92\)), Curium (\(Z = 96\)), and Californium (\(Z = 98\)) all possess atomic numbers lying in the actinoid series (\(Z = 89\text{ to }103\)).
Terbium (\(Z = 65\)) has its valence electrons filling the 4f subshell and lies in the lanthanoid series (\(Z = 57\text{ to }71\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Terbium (\(Z = 65\)) is a lanthanoid rather than an actinoid. Therefore, Terbium (\(Z = 65\)) is the element that is not an actinoid.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - Screening effect order of atomic orbitals

questiontext.text: The order of screening effect of electrons of s, p, d and f orbitals of a given shell of an atom on its outer shell electrons is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The screening (shielding) effect represents the extent to which inner-shell electrons diminish the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and outer-shell electrons. The ability of an orbital to shield depends directly on its radial probability distribution and penetration toward the nucleus.

Step 2: Penetration Power Analysis
For orbitals within the same principal quantum level (same shell), penetration power decreases as the azimuthal quantum number (\(l\)) increases: \(s > p > d > f\). Because s-orbitals are spherically symmetric and penetrate closest to the nucleus, electrons in s-orbitals shield the nuclear charge most effectively. In contrast, d- and f-orbitals are diffuse with complex angular nodal shapes, resulting in very poor penetration and minimal shielding capability.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The screening capability decreases progressively in the sequence \(s > p > d > f\). Thus, the correct order is \(s > p > d > f\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - First ionisation enthalpy order of period elements

questiontext.text: The first ionisation enthalpies of Na, Mg, Al and Si are in the order:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Electronic Configurations
The elements belong to Period 3 of the periodic table with ground-state valence configurations:
\(\mathrm{Na}\) (\(Z = 11\)): \([\mathrm{Ne}]\, 3s^1\)
\(\mathrm{Mg}\) (\(Z = 12\)): \([\mathrm{Ne}]\, 3s^2\)
\(\mathrm{Al}\) (\(Z = 13\)): \([\mathrm{Ne}]\, 3s^2 3p^1\)
\(\mathrm{Si}\) (\(Z = 14\)): \([\mathrm{Ne}]\, 3s^2 3p^2\)

Step 2: Governing Principles of Ionisation Enthalpy
Ionisation enthalpy generally increases across a period due to increasing effective nuclear charge. However, anomalies arise when electrons are removed from particularly stable subshells or subshells of different penetration power.

Step 3: Comparative Analysis
1. Sodium has the lowest nuclear charge among these four elements and readily loses its single \(3s\) valence electron, giving it the lowest ionisation enthalpy (\(496\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).
2. Magnesium has a completely filled, stable \(3s^2\) subshell, and removing an electron requires breaking this stable configuration (\(737\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).
3. Aluminium has a single electron in the \(3p\) subshell. The \(3p\) orbital is higher in energy, experiences greater shielding by the inner \(3s^2\) pair, and is less penetrating than the \(3s\) orbital. Consequently, removing the \(3p\) electron requires less energy than removing a \(3s\) electron from magnesium (\(577\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), making \(\mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Mg}\).
4. Silicon has a higher nuclear charge (\(Z = 14\)) than aluminium and magnesium, pulling the \(3p\) electrons closer and increasing the ionisation enthalpy (\(786\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) above that of magnesium.

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
Arranging the values yields \(\mathrm{Na} < \mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Mg} < \mathrm{Si}\), which is expressed as \(\mathrm{Na} < \mathrm{Mg} > \mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Si}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q05 - Electronic configuration of gadolinium atomic number

questiontext.text: The electronic configuration of gadolinium (Atomic number 64) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Available Orbitals
The element is gadolinium with atomic number \(Z = 64\). The nearest preceding noble gas core is Xenon (\([\mathrm{Xe}]\)) with \(Z = 54\), leaving 10 valence electrons to be distributed among the \(4f\), \(5d\), and \(6s\) orbitals.

Step 2: Governing Principles
According to the Aufbau principle, the \(6s\) orbital fills first with 2 electrons. The remaining 8 electrons enter the \(4f\) and \(5d\) orbitals. Subshells that are completely filled or exactly half-filled possess enhanced exchange energy and symmetrical electron distribution, providing extra thermodynamic stability.

Step 3: Configuration Determination
An arrangement placing 8 electrons into \(4f\) would give \([\mathrm{Xe}]\, 4f^8 6s^2\). However, retaining one electron in the \(5d\) orbital allows the \(4f\) subshell to attain an exactly half-filled configuration (\(4f^7\)), which is exceptionally stable due to maximum exchange energy. Therefore, the ground-state electronic configuration of gadolinium is \([\mathrm{Xe}]\, 4f^7 5d^1 6s^2\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct ground-state electronic configuration is \([\mathrm{Xe}]\, 4f^7 5d^1 6s^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q06 - Incorrect statement regarding modern periodic classification

questiontext.text: The statement that is not correct for periodic classification of elements is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The modern periodic table is structured based on Moseley's Periodic Law and the Aufbau principle for electron configuration, where orbitals are filled in order of increasing \((n+l)\) energy value.

Step 2: Evaluation of Statements
1. According to the modern periodic law, physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. This statement is correct.
2. More than 78% of all known elements are metals located on the left and central parts of the periodic table; non-metals are fewer than 20 and reside at the top right. Thus, non-metallic elements are indeed fewer in number than metallic elements. This statement is correct.
3. According to the Aufbau principle, the \((n+l)\) energy rule establishes that the \(4s\) orbital (\(n+l = 4+0 = 4\)) has lower energy than the \(3d\) orbital (\(n+l = 3+2 = 5\)). Therefore, electrons fill the \(4s\)-orbital after \(3p\) and before the \(3d\)-orbitals, not the other way around. Thus, stating that \(3d\)-orbitals are filled before \(4s\)-orbitals is false.
4. Across a period from left to right, effective nuclear charge increases, contracting atomic size and holding valence electrons more tightly, which causes the first ionisation enthalpy to generally increase. This statement is correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion that \(3d\)-orbitals are filled with electrons after \(3p\)-orbitals and before \(4s\)-orbitals is incorrect.

answer.text: The properties of elements are periodic function of their atomic numbers.
Non metallic elements are less in number than metallic elements.
For transition elements, the 3d-orbitals are filled with electrons after 3p-orbitals and before 4s-orbitals.
The first ionisation enthalpies of elements generally increase with increase in atomic number as we go along a period.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q07 - Energy released in electron gain of halogens

questiontext.text: Among halogens, the correct order of amount of energy released in electron gain (electron gain enthalpy) is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electron gain enthalpy (\(\Delta_{\text{eg}}H\)) reflects the energy change when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron. The amount of energy released corresponds to the magnitude of negative electron gain enthalpy. Generally, electron gain enthalpy becomes less negative down a group as atomic radius increases and attraction for the added electron decreases.

Step 2: Analysis of the Group 17 Anomaly
Fluorine is situated in Period 2 with a very small and compact \(2p\) subshell. The addition of an extra electron results in strong interelectronic repulsions within this small volume, which offsets some of the electrostatic stabilization. In contrast, chlorine has a larger \(3p\) subshell where incoming electrons experience significantly less electron-electron repulsion. Consequently, more energy is released upon adding an electron to chlorine (\(-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) than to fluorine (\(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 3: Trend Down the Rest of the Group
From chlorine to bromine and iodine, size increases regularly and the distance between the nucleus and the valence shell increases, decreasing the energy released: \(\mathrm{Cl} (-349) > \mathrm{F} (-328) > \mathrm{Br} (-325) > \mathrm{I} (-295\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The energy released follows the sequence \(\mathrm{Cl} > \mathrm{F} > \mathrm{Br} > \mathrm{I}\), which is represented as \(\mathrm{F} < \mathrm{Cl} > \mathrm{Br} > \mathrm{I}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q08 - Period number equality in modern periodic table

questiontext.text: The period number in the long form of the periodic table is equal to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the modern periodic table, horizontal rows are called periods. Each period begins with the filling of the valence shell corresponding to a new principal quantum number (\(n\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Quantum Numbers
The principal quantum number \(n\) defines the main energy level or shell being populated. For any given element across a period, electrons enter subshells belonging to principal quantum levels up to a maximum value \(n_{\text{max}}\). For example, in the 4th period, \(n = 4\) is the highest principal quantum number (filling \(4s\), \(3d\), and \(4p\)). Therefore, the period number corresponds precisely to the maximum principal quantum number (\(n\)) of any element of that period.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The period number in the long form of the periodic table is equal to the maximum principal quantum number of any element of the period.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q09 - Elements with progressive filling of four f orbital

questiontext.text: The elements in which electrons are progressively filled in 4f-orbital are called

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The f-block elements are characterized by the progressive filling of electrons into the inner \((n-2)f\) subshells and are categorized into two distinct series: the lanthanoid series and the actinoid series.

Step 2: Evaluation of Series
1. The series in which electrons progressively fill the \(4f\) subshell consists of 14 elements following lanthanum (cerium, \(Z=58\), through lutetium, \(Z=71\)), known collectively as lanthanoids.
2. The series in which electrons progressively fill the \(5f\) subshell consists of 14 elements following actinium (thorium, \(Z=90\), through lawrencium, \(Z=103\)), known as actinoids.
3. Transition elements involve the progressive filling of \(d\)-orbitals, while halogens involve the filling of \(p\)-orbitals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Elements in which the \(4f\)-orbitals are progressively filled are called lanthanoids.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q10 - Correct order of size of iodine species

questiontext.text: Which of the following is the correct order of size of the given species:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Species and Condition
The given species are the iodide anion (\(\mathrm{I^{-}}\)), neutral iodine atom (\(\mathrm{I}\)), and the iodonium cation (\(\mathrm{I^{+}}\)). All three species possess the same nuclear charge (\(Z = 53\) protons).

Step 2: Governing Principles of Atomic and Ionic Radii
1. Cation formation involves the loss of one or more electrons from the valence shell, reducing electron-electron repulsions and increasing the effective nuclear charge per electron. This pulls the remaining electrons closer to the nucleus, resulting in a radius smaller than that of the neutral parent atom: \(r_{\text{cation}} < r_{\text{atom}}\).
2. Anion formation involves the addition of one or more electrons, increasing electron-electron repulsions and expanding the electron cloud. The effective nuclear charge per electron decreases, causing the radius to exceed that of the neutral parent atom: \(r_{\text{anion}} > r_{\text{atom}}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Comparison
Combining these effects gives: \(\mathrm{I^{-}} > \mathrm{I} > \mathrm{I^{+}}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
The anion with 54 electrons is the largest, the neutral atom with 53 electrons is intermediate, and the cation with 52 electrons is the smallest. Therefore, the correct order of size is \(\mathrm{I^{-}} > \mathrm{I} > \mathrm{I^{+}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q11 - Unfavourable formation of oxide ion in gas phase

questiontext.text:
The formation of the oxide ion, \(\mathrm{O^{2-} (g)}\), from oxygen atom requires first an exothermic and then an endothermic step as shown below:

\[\mathrm{O (g) + e^{-} \longrightarrow O^{-} (g); \quad \Delta H^{\circ} = - 141 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}\]\[\mathrm{O^{-} (g) + e^{-} \longrightarrow O^{2-} (g); \quad \Delta H^{\circ} = + 780 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}\]

Thus process of formation of \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) in gas phase is unfavourable even though \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) is isoelectronic with neon. It is due to the fact that,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The first electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is exothermic because the neutral oxygen atom has high electronegativity and the incoming electron experiences net attraction from the nucleus. However, the second electron gain enthalpy is strongly endothermic because an electron is added to a species that already carries a negative charge (\(\mathrm{O^{-}}\)).

Step 2: Force Balance Analysis
When an electron approaches the negatively charged \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) ion, strong electrostatic repulsive forces operate between like negative charges. Overcoming this severe electrostatic repulsion requires a substantial input of energy (\(+780\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). Although the resulting \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) ion acquires the stable closed-shell configuration of neon (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\)), this electronic stabilization is far smaller in magnitude than the energy penalty imposed by electrostatic repulsion in the gas phase.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The gas-phase formation of \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) is unfavourable because electron repulsion outweighs the stability gained by achieving a noble gas configuration.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q12A - Block of element with atomic number fifty seven

questiontext.text:
Comprehension:

In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers which is related to the electronic configuration. Depending upon the type of orbitals receiving the last electron, the elements in the periodic table have been divided into four blocks, viz, s, p, d and f. The modern periodic table consists of 7 periods and 18 groups. Each period begins with the filling of a new energy shell. In accordance with the Aufbau principle, the seven periods (1 to 7) have 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 and 32 elements respectively. The seventh period is still incomplete. To avoid the periodic table being too long, the two series of f-block elements, called lanthanoids and actinoids are placed at the bottom of the main body of the periodic table.

The element with atomic number 57 belongs to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Configuration
The element has atomic number \(Z = 57\), which corresponds to Lanthanum (\(\mathrm{La}\)). Its ground-state electronic configuration is \([\mathrm{Xe}]\, 5d^1 6s^2\).

Step 2: Block Determination Rule
An element is classified into a block based on the type of subshell that receives the differentiating (last) valence electron. In lanthanum, the differentiating electron enters the \(5d\) orbital rather than the \(4f\) orbital. The subsequent elements from cerium (\(Z = 58\)) to lutetium (\(Z = 71\)) progressively fill the \(4f\) subshell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the last electron enters a \(d\)-orbital, lanthanum (\(Z = 57\)) belongs to the d-block.

In accordance with the Aufbau principle, the seven periods (1 to 7) have 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 and 32 elements respectively. The seventh period is still incomplete. To avoid the periodic table being too long, the two series of f-block elements, called lanthanoids and actinoids are placed at the bottom of the main body of the periodic table.

The last element of the p-block in 6th period is represented by the outermost electronic configuration.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the Element
The 6th period accommodates elements filling the \(6s\), \(4f\), \(5d\), and \(6p\) orbitals. The p-block contains elements with valence configurations spanning \(ns^2 np^1\) to \(ns^2 np^6\). The final element of the p-block in the 6th period is the noble gas Radon (\(\mathrm{Rn}\), \(Z = 86\)).

Step 2: Electronic Configuration Analysis
For period \(n = 6\), the subshells filled up to the end of the p-block are:
\(6s^2\), followed by the complete \(4f\) series (\(4f^{14}\)), the complete \(5d\) series (\(5d^{10}\)), and finally the complete \(6p\) subshell (\(6p^6\)).
Arranging these valence subshells in standard order yields \(4f^{14} 5d^{10} 6s^2 6p^6\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The outermost electronic configuration of the last element of the p-block in the 6th period is \(4f^{14} 5d^{10} 6s^2 6p^6\).

Which of the elements whose atomic numbers are given below, cannot be accommodated in the present set up of the long form of the periodic table?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The present long form of the periodic table consists of 7 periods with a total capacity for 118 elements (ending at Oganesson, \(Z = 118\) at the end of Period 7).

Step 2: Evaluation of Atomic Numbers

2. Bohrium (\(Z = 107\)) is a transition element in Period 7.
3. Oganesson (\(Z = 118\)) is the final noble gas completing Period 7.
4. An element with atomic number \(Z = 126\) would exceed the maximum capacity of 118 elements of the 7-period periodic table and would require an eighth period (and the start of a g-block).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The element with atomic number 126 cannot be accommodated in the present set up of the 7-period long form of the periodic table.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q13 - Increasing tendency to gain electron among configurations

questiontext.text:
Electronic configurations of four elements A, B, C and D are given below :

(A) \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\)
(B) \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^4\)
(C) \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1\)
(D) \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^5\)

Which of the following is the correct order of increasing tendency to gain electron :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the Elements from Given Configurations
Element A: \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\) is Neon (\(\mathrm{Ne}\)), a noble gas with a completely filled, exceptionally stable octet.
Element B: \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^4\) is Oxygen (\(\mathrm{O}\)), a non-metal requiring two electrons to complete its valence octet.
Element C: \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1\) is Sodium (\(\mathrm{Na}\)), an alkali metal with a strong tendency to lose its single \(3s\) valence electron rather than gain electrons.
Element D: \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^5\) is Fluorine (\(\mathrm{F}\)), a halogen requiring only one electron to achieve a noble gas configuration.

Step 2: Evaluating Tendency to Gain an Electron
1. Element A (noble gas) has a positive electron gain enthalpy and zero affinity for an extra electron, giving it the lowest tendency to gain an electron.
2. Element C (alkali metal) has a low electropositive character and a slightly negative electron gain enthalpy, but its electropositive nature makes its tendency to gain an electron very low, though higher than an inert gas.
3. Element B (group 16 non-metal) has a high negative electron gain enthalpy (\(-141\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) and a strong tendency to accept electrons.
4. Element D (halogen) has the highest electronegativity and a very large negative electron gain enthalpy (\(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), giving it the strongest driving force to gain an electron.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Arranging the elements in order of increasing tendency to gain an electron gives \(\mathrm{A} < \mathrm{C} < \mathrm{B} < \mathrm{D}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q14 - Elements capable of showing covalency greater than four

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements can show covalency greater than 4?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The maximum covalency of an element depends on the number of valence orbitals available for bonding in its outer shell. Second-period elements have only \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals in their valence shell (a total of four orbitals) and lack d-orbitals, restricting their maximum covalency strictly to 4. Third-period and heavier elements possess vacant \(d\)-orbitals, allowing expansion of their octet and exhibition of covalencies greater than 4.

Step 2: Evaluation of Given Elements
1. Beryllium (\(\mathrm{Be}\)) and Boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)) belong to the second period (principal quantum number \(n = 2\)), where no \(d\)-orbitals exist. Their maximum covalency cannot exceed 4.
2. Phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}\)) and Sulfur (\(\mathrm{S}\)) belong to the third period (\(n = 3\)), having accessible, energetically vacant \(3d\)-orbitals in addition to \(3s\) and \(3p\) orbitals. For instance, phosphorus exhibits a covalency of 5 in \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\), and sulfur exhibits a covalency of 6 in \(\mathrm{SF_6}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Phosphorus and sulfur can expand their coordination spheres and display covalencies greater than 4.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q15 - Groups of elements imparting characteristic flame colour

questiontext.text: Those elements impart colour to the flame on heating in it, the atoms of which require low energy for the ionisation (i.e., absorb energy in the visible region of spectrum). The elements of which of the following groups will impart colour to the flame?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When elements are introduced into a flame, thermal energy excites their valence electrons to higher energy levels. When these excited electrons fall back to the ground state, energy is emitted as visible light, producing characteristic flame colours. This phenomenon occurs readily in elements with large atomic radii and very low ionisation enthalpies.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Groups
1. Group 1 (alkali metals) and Group 2 (alkaline earth metals, especially Ca, Sr, Ba) have relatively large atomic sizes and very low first and second ionisation enthalpies. The thermal energy of a Bunsen flame is sufficient to excite their valence electrons, causing them to emit characteristic visible light (e.g., sodium yields yellow, potassium yields lilac, calcium yields brick red).
2. Elements in Group 13 and Group 17 have significantly smaller atomic radii and substantially higher ionisation enthalpies. Their valence electrons cannot be readily excited by the heat of a standard burner flame, so they do not exhibit characteristic flame coloration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Elements belonging to Group 1 and Group 2 possess low ionisation energies that allow them to impart colour to a flame.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q16 - Sequences containing atomic numbers of representative elements

questiontext.text: Which of the following sequences contain atomic numbers of only representative elements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Representative (or main group) elements are elements belonging to the s-block and p-block (Groups 1, 2, and 13 to 18), in which electrons are added to the outermost s or p subshells. Transition elements (d-block) and inner transition elements (f-block) are not representative elements.

Step 2: Evaluation of Sequences
1. Sequence with 3, 33, 53, 87:
\(Z = 3\) is \(\mathrm{Li}\) (Group 1, s-block).
\(Z = 33\) is \(\mathrm{As}\) (Group 15, p-block).
\(Z = 53\) is \(\mathrm{I}\) (Group 17, p-block).
\(Z = 87\) is \(\mathrm{Fr}\) (Group 1, s-block).
All elements in this sequence are s-block or p-block elements, so all are representative.
2. Sequence with 2, 10, 22, 36:
\(Z = 22\) is Titanium (\(\mathrm{Ti}\)), which has valence configuration \(3d^2 4s^2\) and belongs to the d-block (transition element). Thus, this sequence contains a non-representative element.
3. Sequence with 7, 17, 25, 37, 48:
\(Z = 25\) is Manganese (\(\mathrm{Mn}\), d-block) and \(Z = 48\) is Cadmium (\(\mathrm{Cd}\), d-block). Thus, this sequence contains transition elements.
4. Sequence with 9, 35, 51, 88:
\(Z = 9\) is \(\mathrm{F}\) (Group 17, p-block).
\(Z = 35\) is \(\mathrm{Br}\) (Group 17, p-block).
\(Z = 51\) is \(\mathrm{Sb}\) (Group 15, p-block).
\(Z = 88\) is \(\mathrm{Ra}\) (Group 2, s-block).
All elements in this sequence belong to s- and p-blocks, so all are representative.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The sequences 3, 33, 53, 87 and 9, 35, 51, 88 consist exclusively of representative elements.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q17 - Elements gaining one electron more readily in group

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements will gain one electron more readily in comparison to other elements of their group?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An element gains an electron more readily when its electron gain enthalpy is more negative. Down a group, electron gain enthalpy generally becomes less negative as size increases. However, second-period elements have extremely small atomic radii, resulting in high electron density and strong interelectronic repulsion when an extra electron enters the compact \(2p\) subshell.

Step 2: Group 16 and Group 17 Comparisons
1. In Group 16, oxygen (second period) has a compact \(2p\) subshell where incoming electrons experience significant repulsion, yielding \(\Delta_{\text{eg}}H = -141\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Sulfur (third period) has larger, more diffuse \(3p\) orbitals with less repulsion, giving a more negative electron gain enthalpy of \(-200\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Thus, sulfur gains an electron more readily than oxygen and other group members.
2. In Group 17, fluorine (second period) similarly suffers from interelectronic repulsion in its \(2p\) subshell (\(\Delta_{\text{eg}}H = -328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), whereas chlorine (third period) provides larger \(3p\) space, resulting in the most negative electron gain enthalpy in the periodic table (\(-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). Thus, chlorine gains an electron more readily than fluorine and other group members.
3. Sodium (Group 1) is an alkali metal that loses rather than gains electrons readily.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sulfur (\(\mathrm{S(g)}\)) and chlorine (\(\mathrm{Cl(g)}\)) gain an electron more readily than the other elements in their respective groups.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q18 - Evaluation of statements on periodic properties and states

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Ionisation Enthalpy of Helium
Helium possesses a closed \(1s^2\) shell with the smallest atomic radius and maximum effective nuclear charge for \(n = 1\). Consequently, helium has the highest first ionisation enthalpy (\(2372\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) of all elements in the periodic table. This statement is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of Halogen Electron Gain Enthalpy
Chlorine has an electron gain enthalpy of \(-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), whereas fluorine has \(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Therefore, chlorine has a MORE negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine, making the statement that chlorine has less negative electron gain enthalpy incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of Physical States at Room Temperature
At standard room temperature (298 K), mercury (\(\mathrm{Hg}\)) is the only liquid metal and bromine (\(\mathrm{Br_2}\)) is the only liquid non-metal. This statement is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Atomic Radii Across Periods
Across any period from left to right, effective nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same principal shell, causing atomic radius to decrease progressively. Therefore, among chemically bonded elements in any period, alkali metals have the lowest effective nuclear charge and the largest atomic radius. This statement is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The statements regarding helium's highest first ionisation enthalpy, the liquid states of mercury and bromine at room temperature, and alkali metals possessing the highest atomic radius in any period are all correct.

answer.text: Helium has the highest first ionisation enthalpy in the periodic table.
Chlorine has less negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine.
Mercury and bromine are liquids at room temperature.
In any period, atomic radius of alkali metal is the highest.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q19 - Identification of sets containing only isoelectronic ions

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets contain only isoelectronic ions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Isoelectronic species contain the exact same total number of electrons. In addition, the prompt specifically requires sets containing only ions (charged species).

Step 2: Electron Count for Each Set
1. Set \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}, Ca^{2+}, Ga^{3+}, Al^{3+}}\):
\(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\): \(30 - 2 = 28\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\): \(20 - 2 = 18\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{Ga^{3+}}\): \(31 - 3 = 28\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\): \(13 - 3 = 10\) electrons.
The electron counts differ, so this set is not isoelectronic.
2. Set \(\mathrm{K^+, Ca^{2+}, Sc^{3+}, Cl^-}\):
\(\mathrm{K^+}\): \(19 - 1 = 18\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\): \(20 - 2 = 18\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\): \(21 - 3 = 18\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{Cl^-}\): \(17 + 1 = 18\) electrons.
All species are ions and each has exactly 18 electrons; thus, all are isoelectronic ions.
3. Set \(\mathrm{P^{3-}, S^{2-}, Cl^-, K^+}\):
\(\mathrm{P^{3-}}\): \(15 + 3 = 18\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\): \(16 + 2 = 18\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{Cl^-}\): \(17 + 1 = 18\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{K^+}\): \(19 - 1 = 18\) electrons.
All species are ions and each contains 18 electrons; thus, all are isoelectronic ions.
4. Set \(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}, Ar, Cr^{3+}, V^{5+}}\):
\(\mathrm{Ar}\) is a neutral atom rather than an ion, and \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) has \(24 - 3 = 21\) electrons. Thus, they are not isoelectronic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The sets \(\mathrm{K^+, Ca^{2+}, Sc^{3+}, Cl^-}\) and \(\mathrm{P^{3-}, S^{2-}, Cl^-, K^+}\) contain only isoelectronic ions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q20 - Periodic property orders not agreeing with given variations

questiontext.text: In which of the following options order of arrangement does not agree with the variation of property indicated against it?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Ionic Size Order
The ions \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}, \mathrm{Mg^{2+}}, \mathrm{Na^+}, \mathrm{F^-}\) form an isoelectronic series with 10 electrons each. As nuclear charge decreases from \(Z = 13\) (Al) to \(Z = 9\) (F), the electron cloud expands, so ionic radius increases: \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}} < \mathrm{Mg^{2+}} < \mathrm{Na^+} < \mathrm{F^-}\). This order correctly agrees with increasing ionic size.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Ionisation Enthalpy Order
Across Period 2, nitrogen has an electronic configuration of \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^3\) with an exactly half-filled, exceptionally stable \(2p\) subshell. Oxygen has configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^4\), where removing one electron yields the stable half-filled \(2p^3\) state and relieves pairing repulsion. Consequently, the first ionisation enthalpy of nitrogen (\(1402\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) is higher than that of oxygen (\(1314\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). The actual increasing order is \(\mathrm{B} < \mathrm{C} < \mathrm{O} < \mathrm{N}\). Thus, the arrangement \(\mathrm{B} < \mathrm{C} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{O}\) does not agree with the property.

Step 3: Evaluation of Electron Gain Enthalpy Order
Due to high electron-electron repulsions in the small \(2p\) subshell of fluorine, chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine (\(-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) vs \(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). In terms of energy released, the order is \(\mathrm{I} < \mathrm{Br} < \mathrm{F} < \mathrm{Cl}\). Thus, the sequence \(\mathrm{I} < \mathrm{Br} < \mathrm{Cl} < \mathrm{F}\) does not agree with the property.

Step 4: Evaluation of Metallic Radius Order
Down Group 1 (alkali metals), the addition of extra electron shells increases the distance between the nucleus and outermost electrons, so metallic radius increases: \(\mathrm{Li} < \mathrm{Na} < \mathrm{K} < \mathrm{Rb}\). This order correctly agrees with increasing metallic radius.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The arrangements \(\mathrm{B} < \mathrm{C} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{O}\) for first ionisation enthalpy and \(\mathrm{I} < \mathrm{Br} < \mathrm{Cl} < \mathrm{F}\) for electron gain enthalpy do not agree with the indicated property variations.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{B < C < N < O}\) (increasing first ionisation enthalpy)
\(\mathrm{I < Br < Cl < F}\) (increasing electron gain enthalpy)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q21 - Properties in periodic classification having no physical unit

questiontext.text: Which of the following have no unit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analysis of Electronegativity
Electronegativity is a qualitative measure of the relative tendency of an atom in a chemical compound to attract a shared pair of electrons toward itself. It is assessed on arbitrary empirical scales (such as the Pauling, Mulliken-Jaffe, or Allred-Rochow scales) and is a dimensionless quantity without physical units.

Step 2: Analysis of Enthalpy Quantities
Electron gain enthalpy and ionisation enthalpy are thermodynamic thermodynamic energy quantities representing energy absorbed or released per mole of substance. Both are expressed in physical units such as \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(\text{kcal mol}^{-1}\), or \(\text{eV atom}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Analysis of Metallic Character
Metallic character describes the chemical tendency of an element to lose electrons (electropositivity) and behave as a metal. It is a qualitative, comparative descriptive property and does not possess a measurable physical dimension or unit.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Electronegativity and metallic character are qualitative, dimensionless properties that have no units.
